summary: Ground small/medium-object tasks in home/service-robot application literature

findings.summary:
Dobb-E doesn't publish a formal per-skill count table, but the example tasks (open blinds, open drawer, pour marshmallows, pick/place spice bottle, turn knob, close cabinet door, open air fryer, pick/place plate) clearly characterize its skill spread, which I can report qualitatively. I have enough verified data across all systems to synthesize. Returning the final report.

---

# Home / Domestic Mobile-Manipulation Action Vocabulary — Ranked by Prevalence

## The ranked vocabulary (across systems)

**1. PICK + PLACE (pick-and-place / pick-and-drop) — overwhelmingly dominant.** This is the core, and often *only*, manipulation action in the open-vocabulary home systems:
- **OK-Robot**: zero-shot framework is *literally* "language-conditioned **pick-and-drop**" — nothing else. Tested in 10 real homes on 170+ objects; 58.5% success (~1.8x prior OVMM SOTA). [arxiv.org/abs/2401.12202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12202), [ok-robot.github.io](https://ok-robot.github.io/)
- **HomeRobot / Habitat OVMM**: task is exactly *"move the <object> from the <start_receptacle> to the <goal_receptacle>"* — **pick-and-place only**, no open/close/pour. [ovmm.github.io](https://ovmm.github.io/)
- **TidyBot**: primitives are **`pick_and_place`** and **`pick_and_toss`** ("well-suited for household cleanup"); 70 unseen test objects across 8 scenarios, **85.0%** put-away success. [tidybot.cs.princeton.edu/paper.pdf](https://tidybot.cs.princeton.edu/paper.pdf)

**2. MOVE-OBJECT-NEAR / rearrange — the single largest skill bucket in RT-1.** From RT-1 Table 1 (744 total tasks), verified across the arXiv HTML and ar5iv mirrors [arxiv.org/html/2212.06817](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.06817):

| Skill | Tasks | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **Move Object Near Object** | **337** | **45%** |
| Pick from Receptacle & Place on Counter | 162 | 22% |
| Pick Object | 130 | 17% |
| Place Object into Receptacle | 84 | 11% |
| Place Object Upright | 8 | 1% |
| Knock Object Over | 8 | 1% |
| Open Drawer | 3 | <1% |
| Close Drawer | 3 | <1% |
| Long-horizon (multi-step) | 9 | 1% |

→ RT-1's manipulation is ~**95% pick/place/move variants**; open+close drawer is just **6 of 744 tasks (<1%)**.

**3. PUT-IN / TAKE-OUT (receptacle insertion & retrieval).** RT-1: 84 "place into receptacle" + 162 "pick from receptacle." TidyBot's whole job is into-receptacle placement.

**4. OPEN / CLOSE (drawers, doors, cabinets, appliances) — present but rare in scaled systems; central only to Dobb-E.** Dobb-E's example task set is dominated by *articulated openings*: "opening horizontal blinds," "opening kitchen cabinet drawer," "closing kitchen cabinet door," "opening air fryer," "turning knob." (109 tasks / 10 homes, 81% success; HoNY = 5,620 trajectories, 13h, 22 homes — but **no published per-skill count table**.) [arxiv.org/abs/2311.16098](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16098), [dobb-e.com](https://dobb-e.com/)

**5. WIPE / POUR / PUSH / FLIP — appear almost exclusively in bimanual Mobile ALOHA, plus a few singletons elsewhere** (Dobb-E "pouring marshmallows"; RT-1 "knock over").

**6. HAND-OVER / high-five — interaction gestures, niche** (Mobile ALOHA high-five only).

## Mobile ALOHA — the bimanual outlier (7 eval tasks, w/ co-training success) [arxiv.org/html/2401.02117v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.02117v1)

| Task | Action | Bimanual? | Success |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wipe Wine | one arm lifts glass, other wipes | **YES** | 95% |
| Cook Shrimp | flip shrimp w/ spatula while other arm tilts pan | **YES** | ~40% |
| Use Cabinet | both arms grasp/open cabinet, place heavy pot | **YES** | 85% |
| Rinse Pan | grasp pan + turn faucet | partly | 80% |
| Push Chairs | coordinated arms+base | YES (coord.) | 80% |
| Call Elevator | single-arm button press | NO | 95% |
| High Five | gesture | gesture | 85% |

## Takeaway

**Pick-and-place (and its rearrange/"move-near" + put-into-receptacle variants) is by far the most common action — it is ~95% of RT-1's 744 tasks and the *only* manipulation in OK-Robot, HomeRobot/OVMM, and TidyBot.** Open/close and pour/wipe are rare in scaled single-arm systems (open+close = <1% of RT-1; articulated opening is Dobb-E's niche), and the **genuinely bimanual** actions — wipe-while-stabilizing, pour/tilt-while-flipping, two-handed cabinet+heavy-pot — appear almost only in Mobile ALOHA, where one arm stabilizes/holds while the other actuates.

Sources: [RT-1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.06817) · [Mobile ALOHA](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.02117v1) · [OK-Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12202) · [TidyBot](https://tidybot.cs.princeton.edu/paper.pdf) · [HomeRobot/OVMM](https://ovmm.github.io/) · [Dobb-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16098)

I have the academic taxonomy grounding (Krebs & Asfour 2022): bimanual = coordinated vs uncoordinated; asymmetric "one hand stabilizes while the other acts" (stir, cut, pour), symmetric (rolling). This confirms the bimanual classification of pouring/opening containers.

I have all the authoritative sources needed. **Synthesizing the final cited report.**

# Service-Robot Object-Manipulation Action Vocabulary (RoboCup@Home, WRS, tidy-up benchmarks)

## What the canonical competitions actually test

**RoboCup@Home 2026 Rulebook** (the dominant service-robot benchmark) — the manipulation-bearing tests are:
- **Pick and Place Challenge** (kitchen tidy-up + breakfast): *grasp/pick* tableware/cutlery/groceries, *place* into dishwasher/cabinet/trash, *sort* (group "apples with apples"), *open/close dishwasher door & rack*, *pour* milk and cereal. Scoring: "Pour cereal or milk into the bowl without assistance **2×200**"; a "First Pick Bonus … to encourage manipulation"; closing the dishwasher scored "only after at least one item has been placed inside."
- **General Purpose Service Robot (GPSR)**: open-vocabulary commands from the official generator → re-phrased by an LLM. Canonical action verbs are *take/get/pick, place/put, bring/deliver/give-to-a-person, find, follow, guide, tell/answer*. Example command: "Go to the kitchen, find a coke, and bring it to me."
- **Doing Laundry Challenge**: *open washing-machine door*, *retrieve clothes*, *carry* (laundry basket "requiring two arms to carry"), *fold*. Focus stated verbatim: "**Deformable object manipulation, bimanual grasping.**" (6–8 clothes in basket, 2–4 in machine.)
- **Restaurant Challenge**: *take* order, barman *hands over* object to robot, *carry/deliver* to table.
- **Receptionist (HRI Challenge)**: *bag handover* from a guest — "The robot must grab the bag from the second guest['s] hand." Scoring: "Receive the bag from the guest via handover **+50**"; "Requesting handover assistance **−25**"; "Bag placed on the robot structure instead of being handed over **−50**."

(Note: "Carry my Luggage" / "Serve Breakfast" / "Storing Groceries" were standalone tests in 2019–2024; in the 2026 rulebook they were merged into Pick-and-Place + Receptionist, but the underlying actions are unchanged.)

**World Robot Summit – Partner Robot Challenge (Real Space), 2018 & 2020** — two canonical skill tests:
- **"Tidy Up Here"**: *grasp → move → release/place* scattered everyday objects (toys, bottles, kitchen items) into shelves/trays/storage boxes and **drawers** (drawer-opening is a scored subtask). WRS2020 set up **31 objects** to tidy; top teams cleared **~14 on average (max 16)** in 15 min with reported grasp accuracy ~94% and "opening of shelf drawers was successful in all games."
- **"Bring Me" / deliver-a-drink**: *find* a drink on a shelf, *pick*, *carry*, and *hand it over to a requested person*.

**Surveys/benchmarks confirm the same core**: the RoboCup@Home trends survey notes "most manipulation tasks are special cases of fetch and pick-and-place," with pouring, tray transport, and cupboard-door opening flagged as the hard ones; RLBench/SceneReplica and embodied-AI benchmarks center the identical primitives (pick-and-place, open/close cabinets-drawers, hand-over).

## Action vocabulary ranked by cross-competition prevalence

| Rank | Action | Prevalence (where it appears) | Bimanual? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Grasp / pick** | Universal — every manipulation test in RoboCup@Home + WRS; "special cases of fetch and pick-and-place" | Single-arm |
| 2 | **Place / put-down** | Universal — pairs with every pick (into table, shelf, dishwasher, drawer) | Single-arm |
| 3 | **Carry / deliver / bring** | Universal — GPSR, Restaurant, Bring-Me, Pick-and-Place | Single-arm (bimanual only for large/heavy: laundry basket) |
| 4 | **Sort / put-away (categorize)** | RoboCup@Home Pick-and-Place ("group with similar items"); WRS Tidy-Up | Single-arm |
| 5 | **Hand-over to a person** | RoboCup@Home Receptionist + Restaurant; WRS "Bring Me"; scored ±50 | Borderline — receiving can need a stabilizing 2nd hand |
| 6 | **Open/close door, drawer, dishwasher, washing machine** | RoboCup@Home Pick-and-Place + Laundry; WRS Tidy-Up drawer | **Often bimanual** (stabilize body + pull handle) |
| 7 | **Pour** | RoboCup@Home Pick-and-Place/Serve-Breakfast (2×200 pts); survey "particularly challenging" | **Bimanual** (hold bowl + tip container; open lid) |
| 8 | **Fold / deformable (laundry)** | RoboCup@Home Doing Laundry only | **Bimanual** (rulebook: "bimanual grasping") |

## Genuinely bimanual actions (academic grounding)

Per the Krebs & Asfour **Bimanual Manipulation Taxonomy** (KIT, IEEE RA-L 2022), the bimanual class that matters for small/medium objects is **asymmetric / role-differentiated**: "one hand stabilizes an object while the other acts on it." That maps exactly onto the competition actions that are bimanual: **opening a bottle/jar (hold + twist lid), pouring (hold container/bowl + tip), and any open-the-container-then-pour sequence**, plus **folding laundry** (symmetric/coordinated) and **carrying large/heavy items** (e.g., the laundry basket "requiring two arms"). Industry framing (Robotics Center) estimates two-arm capability is needed for the majority of "high-value" home tasks (cited 60–70%), driven by stabilize-and-act and hand-over coordination — though that figure is an industry claim, not a competition statistic.

## One-line takeaway

**Pick, place, and carry/deliver are the universal single-arm backbone of every service-robot competition; the genuinely bimanual actions are the minority but high-value ones — pouring, opening containers/jars and appliance doors (stabilize-with-one-hand-act-with-the-other), folding laundry, and carrying large objects — with hand-over to a person sitting on the boundary.**

## Sources
- RoboCup@Home 2026 Rulebook (PDF): https://robocupathome.github.io/RuleBook/rulebook/master.pdf — and repo https://github.com/RoboCupAtHome/RuleBook/
- GPSR command generator (action vocabulary): https://github.com/RoboCupAtHome/gpsr_command_generator and https://github.com/kyordhel/GPSRCmdGen
- WRS2020 Partner Robot Challenge (Real Space) Detailed Rules: https://wrs.nedo.go.jp/wrs2020/challenge/download/Rules/DetailedRules_Partner_EN.pdf and task page https://wrs.nedo.go.jp/en/wrs2020/challenge/service/partner.html
- WRS2018 Partner Robot Challenge ("Tidy Up Here" + "Bring Me") rulebook repo: https://github.com/wrs-prc-realspace/RuleBook2018
- WRS Tidy-Up benchmark + numbers (31 objects; ~14 avg; grasp ~94%): https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01691864.2022.2115315 (and arxiv tidy-up study https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.03671)
- RoboCup@Home survey "Trends, Challenges and Adopted Strategies" (pick-and-place core; pouring/tray hard): https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.10882
- Bimanual Manipulation Taxonomy, Krebs & Asfour, IEEE RA-L 2022 (stabilize-vs-act, pour/cut/stir): https://h2t.iar.kit.edu/pdf/Krebs2022.pdf
- Bimanual survey / "next frontier" (two-hand task fraction): https://www.roboticscenter.ai/research/bimanual-robot-manipulation-survey and https://www.roboticscenter.ai/blog/why-bimanual-is-the-next-frontier

**Caveats:** Tandfonline survey PDFs were paywalled (403); WRS object/grasp-accuracy numbers come from team solution papers via search snippets, not a fetched primary table — treat the exact figures (31 objects, ~14 avg, ~94%) as team-reported. The 60–70% "bimanual fraction" is an industry/marketing estimate, not a peer-reviewed competition metric.

I now have comprehensive, well-sourced data. I have everything needed: Katz ADL taxonomy, quantitative ADL frequencies, task-preference surveys, dropped-object retrieval data, handover study, and the bimanual bottle/jar opening evidence. Let me compile the final summary.

# Assistive/Eldercare Robotics: Object-Interaction Action Vocabulary for ADLs

## ADL taxonomy grounding
- **Katz Index (Katz, 1963)** — the canonical basic-ADL set: **bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding**. Only one ("feeding" = bringing food/drink to mouth) is a small-object manipulation; the rest are whole-body/self-care. This is why object-interaction robotics largely targets *IADLs* (instrumental ADLs: cooking, fetching, housekeeping) and the *manipulation substrate* of ADLs (reach→grasp→place), not the bathing/toileting core. [Katz Index PDF (geriatrictoolkit)](https://geriatrictoolkit.missouri.edu/funct/Katz_ADL.pdf), [HIGN consultgeri](https://hign.org/consultgeri/try-this-series/katz-index-independence-activities-daily-living-adl)

## Action vocabulary ranked by prevalence (with numbers)

| Rank | Action | Evidence / frequency |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Reach + pick / reach + place** (grasp-and-move small objects) | The dominant primitive. **88 reach-and-pick + 84 reach-and-place per hour** in kitchen video; **~1,800 reaches over 11 hrs — 3× the number of door openings**. ([arXiv 2104.03892](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03892)) |
| 2 | **Open/close doors, drawers, cabinets** (incl. containers) | **94 times/day — the single most frequent named "task"**, spanning room doors, cabinets, drawers. ([arXiv 2104.03892](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03892)) |
| 3 | **Fetch / bring / find-and-fetch (carry object to person)** | Rated "essential" by users with disabilities; survey participants ranked **find-and-fetch and pick-and-place as top requested tasks**. Older adults specifically want robots for "transporting and fetching items." ([arXiv 2101.02750](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02750), [Beer PMC4182920](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4182920/)) |
| 4 | **Use handheld electronics** (remote, phone — pick + actuate) | **2nd most frequent daily task** after doors. ([arXiv 2104.03892](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03892)) |
| 5 | **Drink / pour-and-bring-to-mouth + eat** (the one core Katz object-ADL) | **8.8/day (NTCIR), 4.4/day (MIT)**; "drinking, eating... high priority." Pouring a drink is a recurring assistive demo. ([arXiv 2104.03892](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03892), [arXiv 2101.02750](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02750)) |
| 6 | **Retrieve dropped item from floor** | High-priority, high-frequency *need*: people with ALS **drop objects ~5.5×/day**; powered-wheelchair users **4.9 drops/day** vs 1.6 for non-users. **70%** preferred the retrieval robot (Dusty) over current methods. ([Dusty, PMC3296521](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3296521/)) |
| 7 | **Hand object over (robot→person handover)** | Studied directly with motor-impaired (ALS) users delivering phone/medicine bottle/remote: **88% overall success (97% set-down, 78% hand-to-hand)** — note set-it-down often beats direct handover. ([Choi & Kemp "Hand it over or set it down", IEEE](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5326254/)) |
| 8 | **Turn switch / knob on-off** | **10×/hour** in kitchen analysis. ([arXiv 2104.03892](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2104.03892)) |
| 9 | **Open jar / bottle / sealed container (hold + twist)** | Classic high-difficulty assistive task; older adults explicitly name "holding or unscrewing items"; arthritic/weak hands struggle. **Genuinely bimanual.** ([Beer PMC4182920](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4182920/), [dual-arm bottle opening, PMC11430129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11430129/)) |

**Acceptance caveat:** older adults preferred *robot* help for IADL/object tasks (housekeeping, fetching, medication reminders — **50% pro-robot for IADLs**) but preferred *humans* for body-contact ADLs (eating, dressing, bathing — **only 12% pro-robot**). ([Beer PMC4182920](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4182920/))

## Explicitly BIMANUAL assistive actions
The hold-one-thing-while-acting-on-it class is what fundamentally needs two arms:
- **Open jar/bottle/container = stabilize body + twist cap.** The dual-arm TIAGo++ method: *"the robot picks the bottle with one gripper and grips the cap with the other"* because the task *"inherently requires stabilizing the container while rotating the cap — naturally performed with two hands."* ([PMC11430129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11430129/))
- **Stabilize-while-the-person-acts** (robot holds the container/object so the human's one functional hand can act) — the human-robot analog of the same hold+actuate decomposition.
- Other natural bimanual ADL actions in the same family: peel/cut food (hold + cut), open packaging/zip-lock (hold + pull), pour from a heavy jug into a held cup (stabilize cup + pour).

## One-line takeaway
**Most common:** the reach→grasp→place "fetch/bring" primitive dominates everything (3× door-openings; ~88/hr), with open-container/door and drink/pour close behind, and dropped-item retrieval + handover as the signature *assistive-specific* actions. **Genuinely bimanual:** the small minority where one effector *stabilizes* while the other *actuates* — opening a jar/bottle (hold + twist) is the canonical case, generalizing to "stabilize-while-the-person-acts," pour-into-held-cup, and cut/peel.

Relevant local artifacts: the two fetched PDFs were cached to `/home/michaellee/.claude/projects/-home-michaellee-mclee-affogato/bec99dbf-8036-4ebc-b408-ad71891f0cba/tool-results/` (arXiv 2101.02750 and 2104.03892), but the readable numbers above came from the HTML/ar5iv versions cited inline.

Based on the three research angles provided, here is the consolidated grounding.

# Home/Service/Assistive Robot — Small-Medium Object Action Vocabulary

## (1) Ranked vocabulary (across home-mobile-manip + service-comps + assistive-ADL)

| Rank | Action | Cross-angle evidence | Self-contained? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **pick + place / move-near** | Universal backbone: ~95% of RT-1's 744 tasks; *only* manipulation in OK-Robot, HomeRobot/OVMM, TidyBot; "special cases of pick-and-place" (RoboCup@Home survey); 88 reach-pick + 84 reach-place /hr (ADL) | YES |
| 2 | **open/close** (drawer, door, cabinet, jar/bottle, appliance) | Dobb-E's niche; RoboCup@Home Pick-and-Place + Laundry; WRS Tidy-Up drawer; **94×/day = single most frequent named ADL task** | YES (object's own lid/door) |
| 3 | **pour** | RoboCup@Home (2×200 pts); Dobb-E marshmallows; Mobile ALOHA; ADL drink 8.8/day; survey "particularly challenging" | YES (own contents) |
| 4 | **fetch/carry/deliver** | Universal (GPSR, Bring-Me, Restaurant); top-requested assistive task | partly — carry itself is fine, but "deliver/bring **to a person**" tail is not |
| 5 | **twist/turn knob-switch** | Dobb-E "turn knob"; ADL switch 10×/hr | YES |
| 6 | **fold (deformable/laundry)** | RoboCup@Home Doing Laundry ("bimanual grasping") | YES |
| 7 | **flip/reorient, push, wipe, knock-over** | Mobile ALOHA singletons; RT-1 knock-over (8 tasks); ADL | flip/push YES; **wipe NO** |
| 8 | **hand-over to person** | RoboCup@Home Receptionist (±50 pts); assistive 88% success | **NO** |
| 9 | **sort/put-in-take-out (receptacle)** | RT-1 162+84 tasks; TidyBot's whole job | **NO** (needs 2nd container) |

## (2) Confirm vs. missing

**CONFIRMS the existing set.** Every high-frequency action in the home/service/assistive literature maps onto vocabulary you already have: pick/place/move, open, pour, twist, press (button/switch), insert (remove-insert), fold, flip. No genuinely-common self-contained action is missing.

**Candidates that look common but are NOT self-contained (exclude from a two-hands + one-object dataset):**
- **hand-over** — requires a *person* (receiver). Not self-contained.
- **wipe** — requires a *surface + cloth* (second object/tool). Not self-contained.
- **put-in / take-out / sort** — requires a *second container/receptacle*. Not self-contained. (This is RT-1's #1 bucket, but it's pick-and-place *relative to a receptacle* — the manipulation primitive is already covered by your pick/place.)
- **carry/deliver/fetch** — the locomotion/transport is base-level, and the "to a person" goal is non-self-contained; the grasp is already = pick.
- **stack** — already in your logistics set; needs a second object but you've scoped it there.

## (3) Genuinely BIMANUAL for small-medium objects (stabilize-body + actuate)

Per Krebs & Asfour (RA-L 2022) **asymmetric / role-differentiated** class — "one hand stabilizes while the other acts" — the canonical self-contained cases:
- **open a jar/bottle = hold body + twist cap** — the archetype; dual-arm TIAGo++ "picks the bottle with one gripper and grips the cap with the other… inherently requires stabilizing the container while rotating the cap." All three angles independently name this.
- **open container then pour** — hold container + tip / hold bowl + tip source.
- **twist/unscrew lid** — same hold+rotate decomposition as open-jar.
- **fold laundry** — symmetric/coordinated bimanual (two-hand grasp of deformable).
- **press/remove-insert on a held object** — stabilize + actuate when the object isn't fixtured.

(Non-self-contained bimanual cases — wipe-while-stabilizing, pour-into-*held-cup*, cut/peel — fall out by the person/surface/second-object rule above.)

## (4) One-line verdict

Your current vocabulary (pick/place/move + open/pour/twist/press/remove-insert/fold/flip/stack) is **complete** for self-contained home/service/assistive small-medium-object manipulation — the only frequently-cited "missing" actions (hand-over, wipe, put-in/take-out, sort, carry-to-person) are all **non-self-contained** (need a person, surface, or second container) and correctly excluded; **no addition is justified**.
